place: The form · a joint between boards
title: The mold leaves a signature.
subtitle: A gap in the boards can become a raised line.
summary: Watch material enter a narrow joint in a wooden form. When the boards part, a small fin remains on the stone, along with the suggestion of wood grain.
sceneDescription: Two wooden mold boards drawn apart to expose a pale cast specimen with a narrow raised seam and subtle vertical board grain.
modelNote: A conceptual specimen with an exaggerated seam for visibility. The amount of leakage is prescribed, not calculated from a tested mixture. The timber texture is procedural; it is not copied from an ancient surface.

control.label: Leave a gap between the boards
control.offText: Tight-joint comparison: the boards meet and the modeled fin disappears. Surface grain can still transfer.

steps.name: Join
steps.title: Two boards make one face.
steps.text: The form is assembled from separate pieces. Here a small gap is left between two front boards. Switch it off to compare a close-fitting joint.

steps.name: Pack
steps.title: Material reaches the joint.
steps.text: As the form fills, workable material can enter the opening. Whether a real mix leaks, bridges the gap, or carries only fine paste through it depends on its consistency and particle sizes.

steps.name: Set
steps.title: The gap becomes a thin projection.
steps.text: The material in the joint hardens with the body. The boards' inward-facing grain can also leave shallow relief in the surface that touches them.

steps.name: Release
steps.title: Withdraw the boards.
steps.text: The front boards move away and separate. Their joint is revealed as a positive feature: a fin sticking out from the stone face.

steps.name: Inspect
steps.title: Read the positive and the negative.
steps.text: A void in the form can leave a raised feature; a ridge on the form can leave a groove. That distinction helps turn a visual resemblance into a testable account of how a surface formed.

issues.title: A raised line across a face
issues.mechanism: A narrow opening between mold boards gives material somewhere to protrude, creating a fin when it hardens.
issues.remaining: A surviving ridge can also come from unfinished dressing, a mineral vein, repair material, or differential weathering.

issues.title: Board-like surface detail
issues.mechanism: A form can transfer shallow texture during contact, so a single operation could produce both the face and its fine detail.
issues.remaining: The grain direction and relief need close documentation. A younger render or repair could carry a mold impression too.

issues.title: Similar marks on several blocks
issues.mechanism: Reusing the same form could repeat a distinctive joint or defect on more than one cast surface.
issues.remaining: A useful match needs dimensions and the same irregular details, rather than several roughly straight lines.

hypothesis: This scene isolates one proposed consequence of timber formwork. A seam and its adjacent texture might record contact with a mold, but this invented specimen makes no claim about the origin of a particular ancient block.
alternative: Compare formwork traces with stone-dressing marks, natural bands, weathering, and repair seams. Establish that the feature belongs to the original stone surface before interpreting it as evidence of manufacture.
test: Cast matched specimens against tight and deliberately open board joints. Record mix consistency, gap size, curing, and release. Scan the resulting fins and grain, then compare a documented candidate using the same surface measurements.
